title: relationships between decimals, fractions, ratios, and percents

lesson.title: Four Names, One Amount: Fractions, Decimals, Percents and Ratios

steps.say: Hey, check your phone for a second. When the battery says fifty percent, you know exactly what that means — it's half full. Your water bottle can be half empty, a coach can say you sank half your shots, and a sale sign can say fifty percent off. Same amount every time, just wearing a different outfit. That's what today is about: one amount can have four different names, and once you can switch between them, math gets way easier.

visual.caption: Fifty out of one hundred squares shaded — a half-full battery

steps.say: Here are the four names. As a fraction it's one half. As a decimal it's zero point five. As a percent it's fifty percent. And as a ratio it's fifty to one hundred, which means fifty parts shaded for every one hundred parts in total. Four ways of writing it, one single amount. Think of it like your name, your nickname, your gamertag, and your jersey number — all different, all still you.

visual.caption: One pizza cut in two, one slice shaded — that's the half

steps.say: Here's the secret that connects everything: the word percent literally means out of one hundred. So if you can get your fraction to have one hundred on the bottom, you're done. Take one quarter. One quarter is the same as twenty-five out of one hundred, because one hundred divided by four is twenty-five. So one quarter equals zero point two five equals twenty-five percent. Picture a hundred-square grid with twenty-five squares coloured in — that's a quarter of the grid.

visual.caption: Twenty-five of one hundred squares — one quarter

steps.say: But what if the bottom number doesn't fit nicely into one hundred? Then you just divide. A fraction is a division question in disguise. Three eighths means three divided by eight, and that gives zero point three seven five. The division stops — nothing is left over — so we call that a terminating decimal. To make it a percent, slide the decimal two places right: thirty-seven point five percent.

visual.caption: Three tenths, seven hundredths, five thousandths

steps.say: Now try one third. Divide one by three and you get zero point three three three, and the threes never stop. That's called a repeating decimal, and we write it with a little bar over the three. As a percent it's about thirty-three point three percent. Here's why that's useful: if three friends split a pizza evenly, each one gets a bit less than a half. On the number line you can see one third sitting to the left of zero point five, so one third is smaller than one half.

visual.caption: One third sits to the left of one half

steps.say: Let's use this for real. Say your class joins a shoreline cleanup at a beach here in B.C. Your group picks up two hundred pieces of litter, and eighty of them are plastic. As a ratio that's eighty to two hundred. As a fraction it's eighty over two hundred, and dividing top and bottom by forty gives two fifths. Two divided by five is zero point four, which is forty percent. So plastic was forty percent of everything you collected — that's a headline you could actually put in the school newsletter.

visual.caption: Eighty of two hundred pieces were plastic — forty percent

steps.say: One more, a little trickier. Three classes report how much of their group showed up for the cleanup. Class A says three fifths, Class B says zero point five five, and Class C says fifty-eight percent. Totally different outfits, so change them all into one outfit — percents. Three fifths is three divided by five, which is zero point six, so sixty percent. Zero point five five is fifty-five percent. Class C is already fifty-eight percent. So the order from smallest to biggest is fifty-five percent, then fifty-eight percent, then sixty percent. Class A wins.

visual.caption: Zero point five five jumps up to zero point six — Class A is ahead

steps.say: So here's the whole lesson in one move: when numbers show up in different outfits, change them all into the same outfit — usually decimals or percents — and then they're easy to compare. Fraction to decimal, just divide. Decimal to percent, multiply by one hundred. Percent back to fraction, put it over one hundred and simplify. That's the whole loop, and you'll use it every time you shop, game, or check a stat.

visual.caption: Fifty squares is one half; the next twenty-five squares is one quarter

lesson.answer: Fractions, decimals, percents and ratios are four outfits for the same amount — divide to get the decimal, times one hundred to get the percent, and compare them all in the same outfit.

practice.question: At a shoreline cleanup near Stanley Park, your team collects 50 pieces of litter, and 30 of them are plastic bottle caps. Write the bottle-cap share as a fraction in simplest form, as a decimal, as a percent, and as a ratio of caps to total litter.
practice.answer: 30 out of 50 is 30/50, which simplifies to 3/5. Three divided by five is 0.6, which is 60%. The ratio is 30:50, or 3:5 in simplest form.
